Apple___Apple_scab.summary: Apple scab is a fungal disease that produces olive green to brown velvety spots on leaves, which later turn dark and cracked. Heavily infected leaves drop early, weakening the tree.
causes: The fungus Venturia inaequalis
Cool, wet spring weather with long periods of leaf wetness
Spores overwinter on fallen infected leaves under the tree
treatment: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves to remove the overwintering source
Prune to open the canopy so leaves dry faster after rain
Apply a suitable fungicide from bud break through the wet spring period
Plant scab resistant varieties where the disease is a recurring problem

Apple___Black_rot.summary: Black rot causes circular leaf spots with purple edges and brown centres, often called frog eye leaf spot, along with cankers on branches and rotting fruit.
causes: The fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa
Warm humid weather
Dead wood, mummified fruit and cankers that harbour the fungus
treatment: Prune out dead and cankered wood and destroy it
Remove mummified fruit left hanging on the tree
Apply fungicide during the growing season if infection is severe
Keep trees healthy and avoid drought or winter injury that invites infection

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.summary: Cedar apple rust shows as bright orange or yellow spots on the upper leaf surface, often with small dark dots, and tube like growths underneath.
causes: The fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae
Requires both apple trees and nearby juniper or cedar to complete its life cycle
Wet spring weather that spreads spores from the cedar host
treatment: Remove nearby juniper or cedar hosts where practical, ideally within a few hundred metres
Cut out the brown galls on juniper before spring rains release spores
Apply fungicide during the infection window in spring
Choose rust resistant apple varieties for new planting

Apple___healthy.summary: No disease detected. The apple leaf appears healthy.
treatment: Continue regular monitoring, especially during wet spring weather
Keep the area under the tree clear of fallen leaves and fruit

Blueberry___healthy.summary: No disease detected. The blueberry leaf appears healthy.
treatment: Maintain acidic soil, around pH 4.5 to 5.5, for healthy growth
Keep monitoring for leaf spots and insect damage

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.summary: Powdery mildew coats leaves and shoots in a white powdery film. Affected young leaves may curl, twist or stay stunted.
causes: The fungus Podosphaera clandestina
Warm days with cool humid nights
Dense canopies with poor air movement
Excess nitrogen that pushes soft new growth
treatment: Prune to improve air circulation and light into the canopy
Avoid over fertilising with nitrogen
Apply sulphur or another suitable fungicide at the first sign
Remove and destroy badly infected shoots

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.summary: No disease detected. The cherry leaf appears healthy.
treatment: Keep the canopy open with regular pruning
Watch for powdery mildew in warm humid spells

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.summary: Grey leaf spot produces long, narrow, rectangular grey to tan lesions that run along the leaf veins. Severe infection kills leaf tissue and cuts yield.
causes: The fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis
Warm humid conditions with extended dew periods
Crop residue left on the surface from a previous maize crop
Continuous maize planting without rotation
treatment: Rotate away from maize for at least one season
Bury or remove infected crop residue by tillage
Plant tolerant hybrids in fields with a history of the disease
Apply a foliar fungicide around tasselling if pressure is high

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.summary: Common rust appears as small reddish brown powdery pustules scattered on both leaf surfaces. Heavy infection yellows and dries the leaves.
causes: The fungus Puccinia sorghi
Cool temperatures around 16 to 25 degrees with high humidity
Spores blown in on the wind from other regions
treatment: Plant resistant hybrids, which is the main control
Apply a foliar fungicide if infection appears early and spreads quickly
Avoid very late planting, which tends to meet higher spore loads

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.summary: Northern leaf blight produces long cigar shaped grey green to tan lesions on the leaves. Lesions merge and can kill large areas of leaf tissue.
causes: The fungus Exserohilum turcicum
Moderate temperatures with heavy dew or frequent rain
Infected maize residue left on the field surface
treatment: Use resistant hybrids where the disease is common
Rotate crops and manage residue by tillage
Apply fungicide from just before tasselling if lesions reach the upper leaves
Avoid dense planting that keeps the canopy wet

Corn_(maize)___healthy.summary: No disease detected. The maize leaf appears healthy.
treatment: Keep scouting through the season, especially around tasselling
Rotate crops to keep disease pressure low

Grape___Black_rot.summary: Black rot causes small tan leaf spots with dark borders, and later shrivels fruit into hard black mummies. It can destroy an entire crop in a wet year.
causes: The fungus Guignardia bidwellii
Warm wet weather during the period from bloom to fruit set
Mummified berries and infected canes left in the vineyard
treatment: Remove and destroy mummified berries and infected canes during dormant pruning
Keep the canopy open so leaves and fruit dry quickly
Apply fungicide from early shoot growth through fruit set
Clear fallen debris from under the vines

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).summary: Esca, also called black measles, shows as tiger stripe patterns of yellow or red between the leaf veins. Vines may collapse suddenly in hot weather and berries can develop dark spots.
causes: A complex of wood infecting fungi including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora
Fungi entering through large pruning wounds
Older vines under water or heat stress
treatment: Prune during dry weather and protect large wounds
Remove and burn severely affected vines, since there is no cure once the wood is colonised
Avoid unnecessary large pruning cuts
Keep vines evenly watered to reduce stress

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.summary: Isariopsis leaf spot produces irregular dark brown patches on the leaves, often with a lighter centre. Heavy infection causes early leaf fall.
causes: The fungus Pseudocercospora vitis
Warm humid weather and prolonged leaf wetness
Dense canopies and infected leaf litter
treatment: Improve air flow through canopy management and leaf removal
Clear and destroy fallen leaves at the end of the season
Apply fungicide where infection is regular and severe
Avoid overhead irrigation that keeps foliage wet

Grape___healthy.summary: No disease detected. The grape leaf appears healthy.
treatment: Maintain an open canopy for airflow
Keep monitoring through warm wet periods

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).summary: Citrus greening, also called Huanglongbing, causes blotchy uneven yellowing across the leaf that does not match on both sides of the midrib. Fruit stays small, lopsided and bitter. It is the most serious citrus disease in the world.
causes: The bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter, which lives in the tree's vascular system
Spread by the Asian citrus psyllid insect
Also spread by grafting with infected budwood
treatment: There is no cure. Infected trees decline and should be removed to protect nearby trees
Control psyllid populations with approved insecticides and biological control
Plant only certified disease free nursery stock
Report suspected cases to local agricultural authorities, as this is a regulated disease in many countries

Peach___Bacterial_spot.summary: Bacterial spot causes small dark angular leaf spots that often fall out and leave a shot hole appearance. Fruit develops pits and cracks.
causes: The bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni
Warm wet windy weather that drives bacteria into leaf tissue
Sandy sites and wind exposure that injure leaves
treatment: Plant resistant or tolerant varieties, which is the main defence
Use windbreaks to reduce leaf injury
Apply copper sprays early in the season, following label rates carefully to avoid damage
Avoid overhead irrigation

Peach___healthy.summary: No disease detected. The peach leaf appears healthy.
treatment: Keep monitoring after warm windy rain, which favours bacterial spot
Maintain balanced nutrition and good drainage

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.summary: Bacterial spot produces small water soaked spots that turn brown with yellow halos. Leaves may yellow and drop, exposing fruit to sunscald.
causes: Xanthomonas bacteria
Warm wet conditions and splashing water
Infected seed or transplants
Handling plants while the foliage is wet
treatment: Use certified disease free seed and transplants
Avoid working among plants when they are wet
Switch to drip irrigation instead of overhead watering
Rotate away from peppers and tomatoes for two to three years
Remove and destroy badly infected plants

Pepper,_bell___healthy.summary: No disease detected. The bell pepper leaf appears healthy.
treatment: Water at the base rather than over the leaves
Keep rotating crops between seasons

Potato___Early_blight.summary: Early blight causes brown spots with concentric rings, giving a target like appearance, usually starting on the older lower leaves.
causes: The fungus Alternaria solani
Warm humid weather with alternating wet and dry spells
Plants stressed by poor nutrition or drought
Infected plant debris left in the soil
treatment: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves early
Keep plants well fed and evenly watered, since stressed plants are hit hardest
Rotate crops for at least two years
Apply fungicide preventively where the disease appears every season
Mulch to stop soil splashing onto lower leaves

Potato___Late_blight.summary: Late blight causes large dark water soaked patches on leaves, often with a pale green edge and white fuzzy growth underneath in humid weather. It spreads extremely fast and can destroy a crop in days. This is the disease behind the Irish potato famine.
causes: The oomycete Phytophthora infestans
Cool wet weather, roughly 10 to 20 degrees with high humidity
Infected seed tubers and volunteer plants
Spores carried long distances on the wind
treatment: Act immediately, as this disease moves faster than any other here
Remove and destroy infected plants, do not compost them
Apply protective fungicide before infection when wet weather is forecast
Plant certified disease free seed tubers
Hill soil over tubers to stop spores washing down to them
Destroy volunteer potato plants and cull piles

Potato___healthy.summary: No disease detected. The potato leaf appears healthy.
treatment: Scout frequently during cool wet weather for late blight
Keep tubers well covered with soil

Raspberry___healthy.summary: No disease detected. The raspberry leaf appears healthy.
treatment: Thin canes to keep air moving through the row
Remove old fruited canes after harvest

Soybean___healthy.summary: No disease detected. The soybean leaf appears healthy.
treatment: Continue scouting through the season
Rotate crops to limit build up of soil borne disease

Squash___Powdery_mildew.summary: Powdery mildew coats leaves in white powdery patches that spread until leaves yellow and die. It is one of the most common problems on squash and pumpkin.
causes: Fungi including Podosphaera xanthii
Warm dry days with humid nights, unusually it does not need wet leaves
Crowded plantings with poor air movement
Shaded lower leaves
treatment: Space plants well and remove some lower leaves to improve airflow
Treat at the very first spots with sulphur, potassium bicarbonate or a suitable fungicide
Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves
Choose resistant varieties in future plantings
Water at the base in the morning

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.summary: Leaf scorch produces many small dark purple spots that merge until the leaf looks burnt along the edges and dries out.
causes: The fungus Diplocarpon earlianum
Warm wet weather and prolonged leaf wetness
Crowded beds with poor air movement
Infected old leaves left in the bed
treatment: Remove and destroy infected leaves, especially after harvest
Renovate beds by thinning crowded plants
Use drip irrigation rather than overhead watering
Apply fungicide where the problem recurs
Plant resistant varieties

Strawberry___healthy.summary: No disease detected. The strawberry leaf appears healthy.
treatment: Keep beds thinned and weeded for airflow
Water at the base of plants

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.summary: Bacterial spot causes small dark greasy looking spots on leaves, often with a yellow halo, and raised scabby spots on fruit.
causes: Xanthomonas bacteria
Warm wet weather and splashing water
Infected seed and transplants
Handling wet plants, which spreads bacteria by hand and tools
treatment: Use certified disease free seed and transplants
Do not work among plants while they are wet
Switch to drip irrigation
Rotate away from tomatoes and peppers for two to three years
Copper sprays can slow spread but will not cure infected plants

Tomato___Early_blight.summary: Early blight causes dark brown spots with concentric rings on the lower older leaves first, with yellowing around them. Leaves drop from the bottom of the plant upward.
causes: The fungus Alternaria solani
Warm humid weather
Soil splashing onto lower leaves during rain or watering
Plants stressed by heavy fruit load or poor nutrition
treatment: Remove affected lower leaves as soon as spots appear
Mulch around plants to stop soil splash
Stake or cage plants to lift foliage off the ground
Water at the base, never over the leaves
Rotate crops and apply fungicide preventively if it recurs each year

Tomato___Late_blight.summary: Late blight causes large greasy grey green patches that turn brown, often with white mould underneath in humid conditions. It spreads extremely rapidly and can kill a plant within days.
causes: The oomycete Phytophthora infestans
Cool wet weather with high humidity
Spores carried on the wind from nearby infected plants or potato crops
Infected transplants
treatment: Act immediately, this is the most destructive disease on this list
Pull out and destroy infected plants, do not compost them
Apply protective fungicide ahead of forecast wet weather
Keep tomatoes away from potatoes, which share the pathogen
Improve spacing and airflow, and avoid overhead watering

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.summary: Leaf mould shows as pale yellow patches on the upper leaf surface with olive green to brown velvety mould underneath. It is mainly a greenhouse and tunnel problem.
causes: The fungus Passalora fulva
High humidity above about 85 percent
Poor ventilation in greenhouses and tunnels
Crowded plants and wet foliage
treatment: Increase ventilation and reduce humidity, which is the main control
Space plants further apart and prune lower leaves
Avoid wetting the foliage when watering
Remove and destroy infected leaves
Grow resistant varieties in protected cropping

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.summary: Septoria leaf spot causes many small circular spots with dark borders and grey centres, usually starting on the lowest leaves and moving upward.
causes: The fungus Septoria lycopersici
Warm wet humid weather
Splashing water carrying spores from soil and debris
Infected plant debris left from the previous season
treatment: Remove infected lower leaves promptly and destroy them
Mulch to prevent soil splash
Water at the base of the plant only
Clear all tomato debris at the end of the season
Rotate crops for at least two years

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.summary: Spider mite damage appears as fine pale stippling or speckling across the leaf, which later bronzes and dries. Fine webbing may be visible on the undersides. This is insect damage rather than a disease.
causes: The two spotted spider mite, Tetranychus urticae
Hot dry dusty conditions, which mites thrive in
Plants under drought stress
Broad spectrum insecticides that kill the mites' natural predators
treatment: Spray the undersides of leaves forcefully with water to dislodge mites
Keep plants properly watered, since drought stress makes damage worse
Use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, covering leaf undersides
Introduce predatory mites in greenhouses
Avoid broad spectrum insecticides that make outbreaks worse

Tomato___Target_Spot.summary: Target spot causes small brown spots that enlarge into lesions with concentric rings and a light centre, on leaves, stems and fruit.
causes: The fungus Corynespora cassiicola
Warm humid conditions with long leaf wetness
Dense canopies that trap moisture
Infected crop debris
treatment: Improve air movement by pruning and wider spacing
Remove and destroy infected leaves and end of season debris
Water at the base and avoid prolonged leaf wetness
Apply fungicide where the disease is established
Rotate crops

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.summary: This virus causes leaves to curl upward, turn yellow at the edges and become small and crumpled. Plants are severely stunted and produce little or no fruit, especially when infected young.
causes: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus
Transmitted by whiteflies, particularly Bemisia tabaci
Infected transplants brought into the garden or field
Nearby infected crops and weeds acting as reservoirs
treatment: There is no cure for an infected plant. Remove and destroy it to stop spread
Control whiteflies, since they are the only way the virus moves
Use resistant varieties, which are widely available and highly effective
Protect young plants with fine mesh netting or reflective mulch
Remove weeds that host whiteflies

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.summary: Tomato mosaic virus produces a mottled light and dark green pattern on the leaves, often with distorted, fern like or stringy growth. Fruit may ripen unevenly.
causes: Tomato mosaic virus, which is extremely stable and persistent
Spread mechanically by hands, tools, clothing and contact between plants
Infected seed and plant debris
Tobacco products, which can carry the related tobacco mosaic virus
treatment: There is no cure. Remove and destroy infected plants
Wash hands and disinfect tools thoroughly, as the virus survives a long time on surfaces
Do not use tobacco products when handling plants, and wash hands first if you do
Use certified virus free seed and resistant varieties
Avoid handling healthy plants after touching suspect ones

Tomato___healthy.summary: No disease detected. The tomato leaf appears healthy.
treatment: Water at the base and mulch to prevent soil splash
Keep scouting the lower leaves, where most tomato diseases start
